notes: Green Goods helps communities caring for land and each other access useful tools at a low cost, learn from one another and coordinate support while retaining sovereignty over their knowledge.

Our global vision is that every community, regardless of economic circumstances, can access the tools, infrastructure, knowledge and support to care for land and each other. Local language, governance, ability, connectivity and time matter alongside money. Green Goods is the product, protocol and ecosystem. The proposed OS is a workspace within that wider offer.

Affordability and practical sovereignty are commitments to deliver and test. They are not measured savings or a promise of control over copies already shared. The four agreed pillars are Accessibility, Sovereignty, Trust and Reciprocity, with Privacy, Interoperability and Verifiability essential throughout.

Sources: user-supplied proposition and accepted direction, 8 October 2026 Pacific; .plans/ideas/green-goods-os/pitch-revision.md. slides.name: problem

runs.text: Cost, complexity and knowledge silos consume the effort that should go to the land.
Less time for the land. Fewer chances to learn together.
Problem hypothesis informed by FAO regional evidence; local frequency and severity need discovery.

notes: Cost, complex setup and knowledge silos can leave communities spending scarce time managing systems. Knowledge silos leave useful experience scattered across tools and communities, making it harder to find, carry forward and adapt elsewhere.

FAO's Near East and North Africa regional overview identifies affordability, connectivity, skills, infrastructure and fragmented digital-solution markets as barriers. This supports investigating these mechanisms; it does not quantify their prevalence among Green Goods users or establish a global rate. The consequences shown are a problem hypothesis for participant discovery, not customer testimony or observed product savings.

Different tools are not inherently a problem. The concern is where inaccessible services, incompatible records or missing context create avoidable effort. Existing notebooks, conversations and community practices may work well and should remain part of the comparison.

Source, accessed 9 October 2026 UTC: https://www.fao.org/neareast/main-topics/action-areas/digital-transformation/ (P07 in the evidence register). No financial, market-size or impact statistic is asserted.

runs.text: A lesson learned in one place

Differences are part of the lesson.

notes: Shared knowledge should preserve local context, attribution, consent and differences, and help relationships grow within and across bioregions. slides.name: solution

runs.text: Record work, learn from peers and organize support.
Bring notes, photos and reviews together.
Share chosen lessons and ask for advice.
Choose what stays private and what you share.
Proposed Green Goods workspace building on existing work and funding features; status labels follow the inspected capability ledger.

notes: Green Goods brings practical tools, shared learning and coordinated support into one product and ecosystem. The proposed OS is an accessible browser workspace, with optional capture, local assistance and bounded sensor/import integrations. Manual participation must remain useful without new hardware, AI or public sharing.

The intended participant experience is to keep a useful observation, find and review its context, decide what to share, learn from another community and coordinate needed support. Financial, social, intellectual, cultural and experiential value can all matter. These forms of value are not automatically interchangeable or tokenized.

Current foundations: the inspected Green Goods capability ledger and work modules describe Garden records, work capture/review and support paths with availability limits. Proposed extensions: the connected OS workspace, source-linked local assistance, deliberate knowledge exchange and compatible infrastructure services. Later gated work: broader mesh behavior and expanded protocol integration. The commitment-pooling ledger distinguishes deployed infrastructure from an available product flow. No guarantee of ecological outcome, principal, yield or funding follows.

Sovereignty means meaningful permissions, community authority, portability, recovery and exit. The sharing decision must show exactly what leaves the private workspace. Supporters receive only deliberately shared material; their funding does not confer ownership or AI-training permission.

slides.name: pillars

runs.text: Privacy, Interoperability and Verifiability run through all four.
Agreed principles for this proposal, not certification of the current product. Verifying a source or signature does not establish an environmental outcome.

notes: The user accepted Accessibility, Sovereignty, Trust and Reciprocity as the four pillars on 8 October 2026 Pacific; Privacy, Interoperability and Verifiability remain essential across all four. Affordability supports access, defined rights support sovereignty, and appropriate transparency supports trust. Transparency never requires sensitive disclosure.

Sovereignty means effective community authority, permissions, attribution, portability, recovery and exit. It does not promise exclusive ownership of every contribution or control over copies already disclosed.
Source: .plans/ideas/green-goods-os/pitch-revision.md, Agreed pillars.

slides.name: business

runs.text: Who pays, what they get, and in what order.
Access funding for communities is separate from company revenue.
Services and support first is a recommendation; protocol fees and licensing stay out of the initial model. No price or margin is asserted.

notes: Recommended sequence: fixed-scope service, then paid support, then a curated knowledge service if reciprocal use exists, then compatible kits through local partners if installation pain is proven. Protocol fees and commercial licensing stay out of the initial revenue model. Each hypothesis has its own payer, demand evidence and validation experiment.

The earlier subscription price, fit percentage, ARR and margins were authored assumptions and are withdrawn from this core pitch. Access funding for communities is distinct from company revenue; a sponsor paying for access does not buy community records.

notes: One core story with tailored final asks. Ma Earth: collective funding and education for community-led regeneration, with existing work with Hypercerts and Certified (P01); the ask is a design conversation and a scoped cohort. Hypercerts: open records connecting work, evidence, assessments and support; the SDK is marked under development (P02, P03); the ask is a record-compatibility review that avoids duplicating identity or evidence standards. 5th World: site analysis, design and implementation for regenerative properties (P04); the ask is a bounded delivery-workflow review, with no API or demand established. The BioFi Project at biofi.earth: support for Bioregional Financing Facilities, learning and technical coordination, with design principles that include commitment pooling (P05, P06); the ask is one community-defined use case, and software does not replace a financing facility. Confirm the organization before any outreach.

These organizations already have tools and relationships; the deck demonstrates a useful additional role. They are not customers, and logos are not endorsements. No outreach is authorized. The earlier funding ask is withdrawn; a funding request needs a scoped workplan and reviewed costs.
